---
| Model | Why it belongs on your shortlist | Available implementation | Expected integration |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SVDLUT — ICCV 2025** | My first choice for the quality/footprint/speed compromise. Spatially aware, rather than just a global color LUT. | Official PyTorch implementation and pretrained models; Apache-2.0. | Export the predictor; port the fused LUT/grid application kernel. |
| **LLF-LUT++ — TPAMI, released 2025** | Most directly aligned with developing high-dynamic-range input into a pleasing image, including local detail and contrast. | Official code and pretrained checkpoints; MIT. | More work: LUT application plus multiscale pyramid processing. |
| **BPAM — ICCV 2025** | Another strong local-enhancement architecture: predicts tiny, spatially varying MLPs instead of one global transform. | Official PyTorch repository with a pretrained directory; MIT. | Grid slicing and per-pixel MLP application need careful GPU deployment. |
| **SepLUT — ECCV 2022** | Older, but a useful low-complexity baseline: learned 1D curves plus a 3D LUT. | Official pretrained sRGB and XYZ models; Apache-2.0. | Probably the easiest full-resolution rendering stage to port. |

I’ll check SVDLUT’s release history for a working spatial version, then inspect LLF-LUT++ and BPAM’s official code and checkpoints. The current evidence shows incompatible code and weights; it doesn’t establish how that happened.

There’s no older working SVDLUT version in the official history: all three commits use the same kernels and checkpoints. The later changes only adjust the training scheduler and add a video test.

BPAM looks like the better next candidate for our pipeline. It has separate retouching and tone-mapping checkpoints checked into the repo, and its reference implementation uses floating-point spatial coordinates. LLF-LUT++ is also viable, but its multiscale filtering adds more rendering and memory-management work. I’m checking the configurations before making a firm recommendation.

**No older working SVDLUT release turned up.** Its official history has only three commits; the kernels and checkpoints are unchanged since the initial release. Subsequent changes touched only the training scheduler and video testing. [History comparison](https://github.com/WontaeaeKim/SVDLUT/compare/47cd9707c818288b3b5d716512523d1e1ef092c6...4759030cb6a51641a97f4031f56bc21e032e5cea)

A release mistake is possible, but we can’t establish that. Because the published demo matches the buggy kernel, this is more than a recent typo we can safely fix. There’s still no response to the [upstream report](https://github.com/WontaeaeKim/SVDLUT/issues/2).

**I’d qualify BPAM next**, keeping LLF-LUT++ as the second candidate:

| | BPAM | LLF-LUT++ |
|---|---|---|
| Available weights | Separate retouching and tone-mapping checkpoints, directly in repo | TPAMI checkpoints linked externally |
| Spatial processing | Floating-point grid sampling in the reference code | Multiscale Laplacian filtering |
| Integration outlook | Better fit for our predictor + GPU rendering architecture | More pyramid processing, intermediate buffers, and boundary handling |

Sources: [BPAM implementation](https://github.com/CVL-UESTC/BPAM), [LLF-LUT++ implementation](https://github.com/fengzhang427/LLF-LUT).

That’s an integration recommendation, **not yet a quality verdict**. BPAM still needs the same reference-output, RAW color-space, and memory qualification before replacing A. Our AWB and TIFF-export decisions carry over.

I’ll qualify BPAM next: verify the released checkpoints, test its spatial behavior and photo quality, then check the RAW input convention and GPU deployment path before replacing A.

BPAM’s first photo comparison looks promising: the released checkpoint produces sensible retouching without SVDLUT’s colored-grid artifacts. Separating grid prediction from image rendering also reproduces the reference output exactly.

I’m now checking whether we can render in bands without seams. That matters for 8GB GPUs: the reference implementation allocates 59 coefficient channels per pixel, which is too expensive to copy directly into our full-resolution pipeline.

The ONNX export is promising too: the JPEG predictor matches PyTorch to about one millionth in the rendered output on the initial test.

RAW needs more care. The authors confirm that the tone-mapping checkpoints were trained on Lightroom-generated XYZ images, but don’t fully document that conversion. I also found numerical sensitivity in the 4K checkpoint on synthetic noise inputs. I’m separating numerical effects from banding errors before testing real RAW-derived inputs.

The native probe compiled successfully. I’m checking it on the headless 16 GB A4000 while investigating the RAW checkpoint’s poor output; the JPEG model looks promising, but RAW still needs to pass before we replace A.

The grid predictors run on the headless A4000 with CPU fallback disabled: about 17 ms for JPEG and 8 ms for the 4K tone model at the current 640-pixel test size. Those are predictor timings, not full-image rendering.

I also checked BPAM’s code history. Its slicing update preserves the original math. Next I’m testing whether the tone model’s bad output comes from the input conversion or the reduced test resolution.

The 4K checkpoint still produces severely clipped output at 3840 pixels, in both XYZ channel orders. The 480p checkpoint behaves much more plausibly. I found a small official XYZ demo from the dataset supplier, so I can test that directly and rule out our synthetic conversion.

The official XYZ sample gives us a useful split: BPAM’s 480p tone model produces a sensible image, while the 4K model produces an almost-black result with clipped colored edges. The JPEG predictor also matches the PyTorch render on DirectML within about 0.000002 per channel.

I’m continuing with the working 480p model to check whether it can handle our RAW use case; “480p” is its training size, not a hard input-size limit.

The 480p tone predictor runs on the A4000 in about 68 ms at 1620×1080, with CPU fallback disabled. The banded renderer also matches whole-image rendering in the spatial and halo tests.

Personal RAWs expose another issue: a straightforward linear-XYZ conversion produces overly dark, cool results. I’m checking white-point conversion before deciding whether these weights are suitable for our pipeline.

I found evidence that the dataset’s “XYZ” images aren’t stored as ordinary linear XYZ. On the paired official demo, undoing a gamma near 1.8 brings the reconstructed image much closer to its sRGB counterpart than treating it as linear. That could explain the poor RAW results. I’m testing that conversion on the personal photos; it’s still an inferred convention, not a documented guarantee.

That conversion makes the three personal RAW results much more plausible: the 480p model now brightens faces and shadows instead of crushing them. We have a promising candidate in the JPEG model plus the 480p tone model.

I’m saving the reproducible tests and findings. This qualifies the predictor and reference rendering; applying it inside the existing decode/AWB pipeline and exporting matching TIFFs still remains.

BPAM’s initial qualification is complete, committed and pushed as `317c910`.

- **JPEG model:** sensible results; accurate DirectML inference.
- **480p RAW model:** promising results after correcting the inferred XYZ encoding.
- **4K RAW model:** fails visual checks; excluded.

Tests ran headlessly on the **16 GB A4000**. Predictor times were ~13 ms for JPEG and ~68 ms for 1620×1080 RAW input—not full rendering times. Parity tests and strict Clippy pass.

hmm so where does that leave us, is there a path to getting BPAM working at 4k+ or is it a dead end

**There’s a credible path to BPAM at 4K+; it isn’t a dead end.** “480p” describes that checkpoint’s training resolution, not a hard input limit. We already ran it successfully at 1620×1080.

The path is to use the **working 480p weights at higher resolution**, with banded rendering to bound memory. We’ve verified that banding preserves the reference calculation. The separate “4K” checkpoint is the one producing broken results; we don’t need it to process large images.

Two things remain unproven:

- **Quality at full resolution:** whether the working model’s local adjustments remain good at 4K–24MP.
- **Speed and memory:** full-resolution grid prediction and guide networks still need benchmarking. The timings I reported cover only prediction.

The next useful test is the working checkpoint on full-resolution personal RAWs, through our actual decode/AWB pipeline, on the A4000. That will establish whether we can ship it directly or need to predict smaller grids and apply them at full resolution—which would require another quality comparison.

My last update should have made this distinction clearer: **we rejected one checkpoint, not BPAM or 4K output.**
i thought the design for all of these is "run the model at low res, interpolate the adjustments to full res develop", not so?

Yes—that’s the intended design, and my previous answer muddied it.

BPAM has two parts:

1. **Predict adjustment grids from a reduced-resolution image.**
2. **Apply those grids at full resolution**, using interpolation and small learned “guide” networks that select adjustments based on local pixels.

The wrinkle: its reference implementation reduces input by a **fixed factor**, rather than resizing to a fixed small size. So its predictor still gets larger inputs as photo resolution increases. The guide networks also perform some work at full resolution.

Our intended implementation can predict grids from a bounded-size preview and apply them to the full-resolution develop. **That is the path we should test first.** We need to check that changing the reference’s prediction scale preserves quality and detail.

The broken “4K” checkpoint doesn’t prevent this. We can use the working “480p” checkpoint’s weights; we don’t need a special checkpoint merely to produce 4K+ output.

I’ve rewritten that calculation as vector operations and am rerunning parity checks. I’m also keeping the cached adjustment grids separate from catalog records so large shoots won’t load every photo’s grids into RAM.

The native application kernels now match PyTorch closely: maximum channel error is under 0.000004, including band seams. On the A4000, application plus readback took about 28 ms for the small JPEG fixture and 81 ms for the 1.75 MP tone fixture.

The actual pipeline is now working on the headless A4000, including AWB. For the 24 MP RAW, a warm run took roughly 68 ms to prepare, 19 ms to predict, and 941 ms to apply BPAM at full resolution and read the preview.

I’m checkpointing that working POC, then finishing recipe persistence, full-resolution viewing and recoverable TIFF export. Production A is still unchanged until those pieces are validated together.

The stored-recipe path is now connected to analysis and full-resolution viewing. I’m implementing Finish so it replays those frozen grids into a 16-bit TIFF, rather than predicting again or trying to express spatial edits as Lightroom sliders.

One additional photo hit the existing AWB calibration limit. That should retain A-only, as agreed; I’m making sure the qualification run and production path both preserve that fallback.

The production wiring now compiles through the rendering and engine crates. I’m checking Finish recovery, TIFF precision, and the remaining UI/test integration before running the broader validation suite.

BPAM is now the A path, with the same saved adjustments reused by the viewer and export. Finish also keeps spatial edits out of the RAW’s Lightroom sliders. I’m testing interruption and collision cases so TIFF creation remains recoverable without overwriting another file.

The existing app and core tests pass, and the TIFF encoder round-trips all 16 bits correctly. I’ve added checks for all eight EXIF orientations, frozen-grid corruption, and interrupted TIFF publication. Next is the real-photo export run under an 8 GiB admission ceiling on the headless A4000.

The headless A4000 completed 20–24 MP RAWs and JPEGs under the 8 GiB ceiling. Warm 24 MP development took about 1.1 seconds; full-resolution RGB16 TIFF replay and encoding took about 2.7 seconds. The AWB calibration failure correctly retained A-only.

The first full workspace test run also passed: 938 tests. I’m finishing the new recovery tests and checking exported TIFFs against their previews.

The production checkpoint is pushed. The recovery tests pass, including partial writes, destination collisions, and preserving externally edited TIFFs.

I also caught a storage issue in review: Finish should release its private TIFF copy after successful publication or rollback. I’m fixing that so completed exports don’t permanently consume twice the disk space.

The exported TIFFs reproduce the native previews exactly in all four replay checks, including A+AWB. Independent decoding also confirms RGB16 data, an embedded sRGB profile, and capture timestamps.

Strict workspace lint now passes. The remaining checks cover the viewer’s cached neural variants and the Finish cleanup change.

The viewer’s four rendition combinations pass the cache test, including reuse after the source and grid files are removed. All 41 Finish tests pass too.

I’m running one final end-to-end Finish check on isolated RAW copies: planning, TIFF generation, XMP publication, and cleanup. Finish now journals each completed render immediately, so interruption during a large export preserves that work.

The complete Finish checks passed for A-only and A+AWB. Published TIFF pixels exactly match the saved-recipe rendering, RAW sidecars contain the expected white balance, originals remain untouched, and private TIFF copies are removed.

The final app tests, Finish tests, and strict workspace lint are green. I’m pushing the last validation checkpoint now.

Implemented and pushed to `master` (`721d6f0`). BPAM passed qualification and now powers A.

- RAW/JPEG support, independent A/AWB, frozen adjustments reused throughout.
- Finish exports kept RAWs as full-resolution RGB16 TIFFs, with AWB-only RAW sidecars and recoverable writes.
- TIFF/preview parity, recovery tests, workspace tests, and strict Clippy pass.

Validated through 24 MP on the headless A4000 under an 8 GiB budget ceiling. Physical 8 GB hardware remains untested. Working tree is clean.
How performant is our tiff ex port?

About **2–3 seconds per 20–24 MP photo on the headless A4000**:

| Image | TIFF export | File size |
|---|---:|---:|
| 20 MP RAW | 2.0–2.3 s | 121 MB |
| 24 MP RAW | 2.2–2.7 s | 146 MB |

Those timings include RAW decoding, GPU rendering, readback, compression, and writing the TIFF. **Complete Finish adds cache writes, hashing, and publication**, which I haven’t separately benchmarked.

We reuse the saved BPAM adjustments—no inference during export. Compression runs across CPU cores; independent photos run concurrently within the GPU memory budget.

The clearest optimization opportunity is **file size and disk traffic**: these noisy samples compressed poorly. Exporting onto your slow HDD could cost substantially more than the rendering itself.
